newsitem.title: USA: Latin American stocks outperforming U.S. markets.
newsitem.headline: Latin American stocks outperforming U.S. markets.

text.p: Latin American stocks are outshining sagging U.S. markets these days as they shake off a reputation for roller-coaster volatility.

Analysts said bargain-hunting U.S. investors were turning to American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) and local stocks of Latin American companies in the face of higher U.S. interest rates and Wall Street's downturn.
"The concern over U.S. interest rates tends to drive people into diversification and diversification means Latin America," said Curtis Butler, vice president for emerging markets at Lazard Freres.
The Morgan Stanley Capital International index showed Latin American markets had risen 15.6 percent since the start of 1997 through the close of business Thursday.
By comparison, the Standard & Poors 500 index was up 1.3 percent and the Dow Jones industrial average was only a fraction above where it started the year.

The champion among Latin American markets was Colombia, with a market rise of 25.2 percent so far this year. It was trailed by Brazil -- a darling with investors because of its newly stable economy, big privatization program for government-owned companies, and cheap valuations -- at 22.4 percent.

Latin American stocks also have shrugged off the March 25 hike in U.S. interest rates. As of Thursday, Latin American stocks had fallen 1.5 percent, compared with a 5.2 percent drop in the Standard & Poors 500, according to Morgan Stanley.
The steadiness of Latin American stocks and ADRs is a new feature in a region known for markets that usually magnified Wall Street's ups and downs.
David Chon, Latin American equity strategist at Bear Stearns, said between 1990 and 1995 the average volatility of the region's markets was 3.3 times that of the S&P 500.
For example, a 3 percent drop in the United States would mean a 10 percent correction in regional markets.
Those zigzags have smoothed out as countries in the region have stabilized their economies. The measures include stifling inflation, selling state-owned companies and lowering import barriers.
Also, Latin American companies have benefited from far greater scrutiny from the growing army of analysts that follow them.
One sign of greater confidence came this week when Standard & Poors raised its ratings for Brazilian and Argentine long-term foreign debt.
Although the debt is still below investment grade, the increase provides reassurance that the two economies remain sound, said Geoffrey Dennis, global emerging markets strategist at HSBC James Capel.
A favorite target of investors have been telephone stocks that trade in New York as ADRs and are seen as barometers of their host countries.
For example, ADRs in Telebras, Brazil's telephone holding company, have risen from $76.50 at the end of 1998 to $112.875 at mid-afternoon Friday.
Although Latin American stocks overall remain strong, there are some weak points.

Jay Pelosky, Latin American strategist at Morgan Stanley, said more than half the Mexican, Venezuelan and Chilean stocks in the firm's model portfolio were down more than 10 percent from their 12-month highs.

However, "we believe Latin America will outperform the United States this year and encourage investors to use U.S.-induced weakness to build positions in quality stocks which have suffered significant price declines," he wrote in a report.
